Q: How do safe methods, idempotent methods and an application operation key differ?
spoken: Safety concerns whether the method is intended to change server state; idempotence concerns the intended effect of repeating a request. An operation key lets an application bind a logical mutation to stable content. HTTP method semantics do not prove that a particular implementation is safe, and a key must reject changed content rather than merge unrelated requests.

Q: When should an API distinguish invalid input, unauthenticated access and missing records?
spoken: Use a documented error contract separating malformed input, absent or invalid authentication, authorization failure and unavailable dependencies. The exact status choices must match the API policy, including whether to conceal cross-owner record existence. Stable machine-readable error codes let the client react without scraping prose or exposing internal diagnostics.

Q: Why is CORS not authentication or a server-to-server access control system?
spoken: CORS is a browser policy governing which origins may read certain cross-origin responses. Non-browser clients do not enforce it. Authenticate and authorize the request on the server regardless of Origin. A preflight is a browser permission check for a request shape, not proof that its eventual caller owns the target object.

CORS is a browser policy governing which origins may read certain cross-origin responses. Non-browser clients do not enforce it. Authenticate and authorize the request on the server regardless of Origin. A preflight is a browser permission check for a request shape, not proof that its eventual caller owns the target object.

Engineering case: A backend accepts any bearerless request because its CORS allowlist includes only the official website. A command-line client can still call it directly.

Reasoning under a changed assumption: No. Cookies can be attached automatically under their rules and some cross-origin requests can be sent without a preflight. Apply an explicit cookie and CSRF threat model.

Q: How do cookie sessions and browser-held bearer tokens create different risks?
spoken: A session cookie can be HttpOnly so ordinary JavaScript cannot read its value, but browser-attached credentials require a CSRF policy and appropriate cookie attributes. JavaScript-held bearer tokens can be stolen by successful script injection. Both approaches need expiry, server verification, object authorization and invalidation of user-scoped caches on identity changes.

JavaScript-held bearer tokens can be stolen by successful script injection. Both approaches need expiry, server verification, object authorization and invalidation of user-scoped caches on identity changes.

Apply caller scope before selecting the page and bind cursors to their query contract. Avoid treating an opaque cursor as permission.

spoken: Retry only under a policy that considers method/effect identity, failure class, remaining deadline and attempt budget. Backoff and jitter reduce synchronized retry pressure but do not resolve uncertain commits.
